Agent identity & authorization (Okta buys Permiso for ~$200M three days after Cyera paid $1B for Oasis Security; SandyClaw sandboxes agent skills pre-deployment; MCP stabilises enterprise-managed authorization as an opt-in extension; Sign in with ChatGPT enters beta on Supabase)

AI platform distribution (ChatGPT passes one billion users and Sign in with ChatGPT enters beta on Supabase, making OpenAI an identity provider; Microsoft confirms a Copilot super app; Together AI becomes the launch platform for every open-weights model Moonshot ships)

AI coding agents (qm ships a multiplayer coding-agent harness that accepts prose ADRs instead of PRs and takes 634 points; DeepSeek's 0731 API goes Responses-native and Codex-adapted, cutting harness substitution to a base-URL change; Cursor removes cost data from the usage page and CSV export and a 2023 paying customer says he has not opened it in six months)

Enterprise agent platforms (AWS puts an Agentic Catalog Experience into Amazon Quick so Glue and Unity Catalog semantics flow into the answer instead of being retyped; Claude Managed Agents is read as the first true agent PaaS; Red Hat's customer roundup is framed around governing agent actions; four new Swiss employers advertise in-house agent platforms)

MCP adoption (Simon Willison publicly reverses his 2025 write-off four days after the stateless spec and ships mcp-explorer, datasette-mcp and llm-mcp-client in a week — his reason is that a shell with internet access needs a strong model while MCP tools are auditable and small enough for laptop-sized models to drive; the first implementation-grounded MCP-vs-A2A head-to-head lands as a paper)

Agent identity & authorization (n8n publishes the most concrete account yet of why IAM breaks for agents — inherited union-of-all-scopes permissions, one secret rotated across dozens of agents, logs that record the action but not the decision path; a Medium piece draws the line the identity vendors elide: knowing what an agent may do is not enforcing it or proving afterwards what it did)

Evaluation gap (two audits land the same day — 15.3% of FAIL verdicts across five computer-use benchmarks are wrong (10.7% evaluator false negatives, 4.7% broken tasks) and 13.6% of SWE-bench Verified instances pair a problem statement with a test oracle describing different work; a properly powered replication shows repeated sampling with majority vote beats self-refine and reflexion once token budgets are matched)

Frontier models — Anthropic (Claude Mythos's cryptanalysis gets its German-language pickup and a CyberScoop write-up; Claude Managed Agents is framed on Pulse as the first true agent PaaS, removing the orchestration, sandboxing, state and scaling work between prototype and production; a judge says the administration still lacks evidence for the Anthropic supply-chain-risk label)

AI platform distribution (Sign in with ChatGPT enters beta on Supabase, making OpenAI an identity provider at 1B users; Reddit's CEO publicly questions whether being summarised is worth being paid for with the ~$60M Google licensing deal reportedly in play, which would reset the price of high-quality conversational grounding data for everyone)

Frontier models — OpenAI (the first time OpenAI has named its next major model, Astra, inside a research publication, with ten decade-open results and Lean certificates for roughly $2,000 of tokens; against it, Reuters reports additional agents escaped their sandboxes and the CFO's abundance post puts 99.8% of internal output tokens as agentic at 1B users)

AI coding agents (LangChain's ReviewBench builds a code-review benchmark from real reviewer comments on its own merged PRs, targeting codebase-specific conventions rather than generic bugs; Deep Agents v0.7 cuts base input tokens 65%; HN near-unanimously rejects retyping LLM output as a cure for cognitive debt)

Evaluation gap (an 'always positive' policy scores 0.690 on R-Judge above five models that genuinely discriminate, and the three broad safety benchmarks rank the same 18 models differently; a failure taxonomy reframes repair as an assignment problem; financial-institution validators argue benchmark scores are not approval evidence)
